draft.title: Buddhist ethics
card: These are five training rules for daily conduct. Buddhists take them on as a personal commitment, not as commands from a god.

The first precept is to avoid harming living beings. The second is to avoid taking what is not given, which includes stealing. The other three cover sexual conduct, false speech and intoxicating substances that cloud the mind.
Karma means intentional action. Buddhists teach that actions have results, so good intentions and deeds tend to lead to good results, and harmful ones to suffering.
Karma is a link between actions and their results. It is not a judge handing out rewards and punishments.
draft.remember: The Five Precepts guide how to act. Karma explains why actions bring results.

a.q: A Buddhist returns a wallet she finds instead of keeping the money. Which precept does this follow?
opts: Avoiding taking what is not given
Avoiding harming living beings
Avoiding false speech
Avoiding intoxicating substances
a.why: The wallet belongs to someone else, so keeping it would be taking what is not given. Avoiding harm is a different precept, and it does not cover this case, because no one is physically hurt by the choice.

b.q: Kenji, a Buddhist, says his kind choices will lead to good results for him over time. Which idea is he relying on?
opts: Karma, the link between actions and their results
The Five Precepts, which promise rewards for obeying
A god who judges each person's actions
The Eightfold Path, which sets out five rules
b.why: Karma is the teaching that intentional actions lead to results. The Precepts guide conduct, but they are training rules and not a system of rewards. Karma is also not a god judging people.
b.clue: Which idea links actions to their results?

a.best: Avoiding taking what is not given

b.best: Karma, the link between actions and their results
